what-you-run.text: You have cloned nothing, and you want to know a Singular release is what it says it is before you run it: that the files are the ones published, that the release names the formal model its evidence was checked against, and that the singular command built from it runs a registry from creation to termination. One command answers all three from the downloaded bytes alone, and either passes or refuses by name.

You need Nix with flakes enabled, and nothing else: no checkout, no credentials, no running node. You run the verify release app of the release you are checking, and name that release again as the one to download.

A table lists the three assets it downloads from the release page without logging in: the on-chain archive, with the compiled validators, the off-chain source and its own flake, and the run page of the registry commands; the documentation archive; and the checksum file covering both.

The archive is unpacked into a fresh temporary directory, never inside a checkout. The work option chooses that directory and keeps what the run leaves there: the assets, the extracted archive, and the receipt of every command.

what-it-checks-in-order.text: Each check runs only when the ones before it passed, and the first failure ends the run with one line naming why.

A diagram shows the order. Download the three assets. Check the sums of both archives and of every file inside the on-chain archive. Check that the archive names the model commit the conformance evidence reads. Check that the run page, the off-chain flake, the command source and the compiled blueprint are present. Build singular and a development node from the archive's own flake. Then run create, insert, update, terminate and inspect as separate processes on one development network. A failure at each step leads to its own refusal: download failed, sum mismatch, model revision missing or mismatch, member missing, and command failed for the build or the journey.

The model revision is the commit of the application model, the formal specification the conformance evidence reads its statements at. The archive states it as its MODEL-REVISION file, and the verifier compares it with the revision the same release's conformance evidence is compiled against.

The journey is the one on the archive's run page: a registry created, a key inserted, its payload updated and the key terminated, each a separate singular process on a development network the verifier starts and stops itself, with an inspect after every write.

what-a-refusal-means.text: A refusal is one line naming it, and the exit status is one.

A table explains each refusal. Download failed: an asset could not be downloaded; check the tag and that you can reach GitHub. Sum mismatch: an archive, the checksum list, or a file inside the on-chain archive disagrees; do not use these files. Model revision missing: the archive states no model revision, as every release before v0.8.0. Model revision mismatch: the archive names a different model commit from the conformance evidence; do not rely on it. Member missing: a file the verification needs is absent. Command failed: building singular, or a command of the journey, failed; the detail names the step and the work directory keeps every receipt.
A release that passes prints its tag, both archive checksums, the model revision, and the directory it was verified in.

checking-files-you-already-have.text: If you downloaded the three assets yourself, the assets option points the verifier at their directory, and every check after the download is the same.
From v0.8.0 on, the release workflow verifies every release this way, right after publishing it.
